You know, Madam Speaker, when we were elected in 1984, the idea that came to mind when the name Meech Lake was mentioned was that of a place of rest and relaxation. But since the Accord, the words Meech Lake are synonymous with historic agreement. It means team work. It means a great country, Canada, is finally united. I think it is extremely important to have a united country while at the same time respecting Quebec's character as a distinct society. You know as well as I do that Quebec is truly a distinct society within Canada. It is a fact, it has been, is and will be part of our experience. And the 10 premiers representing four different political formations, along with the Prime Minister of Canada, acknowledged that fact, without any partisanship. With the result that Quebec which was entitled to a seat at the constitutional meetings will now have it, a good thing for that province, for Canada and also for all socio-economic and cultural decision-makers who will be able to make progress and think from now on about Canada not as it was in 1982 or 1981 or 1971, but as it is in 1987, that is a country with 10 provinces.
To say that the Meech Lake Accord is not perfect, that changes or such and such amendment should be made, quite simply, Madam Speaker, is to express rejection of the Accord. There has been an agreement. As the Canadian Government, we must sign it as must the 10 provinces. There will be a second round. There will be a second stage where, once again, the 10 Premiers and the Prime Minister of Canada will meet, reassess the situation, improve the Accord if need be, as I think is perfectly normal and logical, but a first step has been taken. That is how a region, a province, a country will grow.

Madam Speaker, first of all, I would like to stress that the Government is proud of the measures taken to protect the purchasing power of workers at the minimum wage since it was elected, and we will remain vigilant in this respect in the future.
The present Government made an in-depth study of its policy on the minimum wage in 1985, after which he announced an increase which brought the minimum wage of adult workers from $3.50 to $4 an hour; this is a 14 percent increase in real terms which came into force on May 26, 1986.
Furthermore, before this review, the minimum wage of workers under 17 was $3.25 an hour, 25 cents or 7 percent below the rate for adults. Since there was a danger that gap might fly in the face of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which prohibits discrimination on account of age, and since this Government remains strongly committed to the principle of equal pay and equal opportunity, we did away with the lower wage rate that applied to the young. The federal minimum wage for workers below 17 years of age was
therefore raised to the adult rate, a significant 23 per cent increase.
The percentages of those two increases, 14 per cent in the case of the minimum wage and 23 per cent for the former youth rate, compare favourably with the 13 per cent increase in the consumer price index since this Government came to power in September of 1984. This last increase in the minimum wage is the first in over six years, since 1981. Currently, the federal minimum wage is more or less at mid-range of the various provincial rates.
This Government takes its role very seriously as regards minimum work standards. In a number of areas, for instance child care leaves, provisions against unfair dismissals, and provisions relating to lay-offs, the Government has assumed leadership. Our minimum wage policy complements our efforts to ensure a basic protection for those workers who are totally or almost totally deprived of negotiating power. That is the thrust of that legislation. We will go on ensuring decent minimum work standards in the interests of all Canadians.
We realize this is not perfect. But I suggest it can be viewed as a step in the right direction.

This might be an opportunity to say a word or two of appreciation for the obvious sincerity with which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) holds his views of opposition to apartheid in South Africa. On this side of the House, we were

all glad to see that the Prime Minister was generally recognized to have shown leadership on this issue, and generally recognized to have held his ground and the common ground of all the other nations of the Commonwealth, except Britain, with respect to the need for preserving those sanctions that are already there, and with respect to accelerating both the substance and the effect of sanctions.
We look forward to Canadian action on that. We not only hope but feel that the Prime Minister, in order to preserve and enhance that perception of integrity on this issue which he came out of that conference with, in a very short period of time will need to indicate what else Canada is prepared to do in order to make good the rhetoric of the Prime Minister.

I hope that the same spirit of independence which imbued the Prime Minister on the occasion of the conference in Vancouver will soon imbue the Government in respect of its attitude toward Central America. I hope, in the same way as we have a Canadian Government ready to speak out independently against apartheid in South Africa, regardless of what Great Britain might think, and to advocate policies which are at odds with what Great Britain might think, that some day we will have a Government which is willing to advocate policies in Central America which are at odds with what the United States might think, a Government free to speak up against continuing American aid to the Contras, a Government willing to locate an embassy in Managua, and a Government willing to increase rather than decrease its aid to Nicaragua.

We look forward to the day when the independent foreign policy perspective which the Prime Minister displayed in Vancouver will be comprehensive.

Mr. Speaker, the denial of the rights of refugee claimants to be heard means that they will be shipped offshore before they are heard. The first test of whether or not they shall be accepted and heard in Canada is the determination that they may have come through what are considered to be a safe third countries. That is what concerns the constituent who wrote to the Hon. Member.
The decision of whether or not a country is a safe third country is done mechanically. The bureaucrats look at a list of countries that are considered to be safe third countries, countries which comply with Article 33 of the Convention. But there have been cases of persons being rejected at Canada's border, sent back to the States and then sent from the States back to their country of origin and there have disappeared. The fact that a country says it complies with Article 33 does not necessarily mean that it does.
This test sounds like a good idea at first, but if we refuse to hear the refugee's story, we do not know whether the third country will be safe for him or whether it will ship him back to his country of origin where he will be persecuted or even killed. The concern raised by the Hon. Member's constituent is a concern which many people have had, and was one of the concerns of the churches, the refugees groups and the law reform groups that dealt with this Act back in its early stages. The safe third country concept does not become a direct violation of the Convention-it is an indirect violation.

October 22, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
structure of Canada which existed long before this document or even the 1982 Constitution. There were undemocratic procedures by which the Government could do anything it pleased, in many cases without parliamentary approval, and often without telling Parliament fully afterwards. I did not have time to add that there is no mandate and no system for having a mandate from the Canadian people. Organizations created by Canadians, like unions, churches, ethnic associations and even political Parties, have no voice as such. They are allowed to speak as individuals. The superboss from Baie Comeau says that they can talk, but he will not pay any attention to them. Those are the deep faults that already existed. They were not created by the Meech Lake Accord, but are illustrated by it.
I am glad the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) asked whether I could cite another constitution in the world that gives special recognition to one district. While I am not a constitutional expert, I know that there is an example. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) would be very pleased to know that in this respect Canada is following the example of Nicaragua.
Nicaragua has established a constitution which provides for autonomy in its eastern departments. This notion is almost unheard of in Latin American governments. It is to allow special arrangements for people who live there, notably Mosquito Indians and other tribes as well as the Caribbean peoples who have settled there. This was an essential means of ending a civil war within that part of Nicaragua and it has been successful.
Unlike the Meech Lake Accord, this was achieved in Nicaragua as a result of two years of intensive house-by-house, town-by-town discussion that resulted in a broad agreement across the country. It is having the effect of bringing to an end the armed conflicts in the eastern part of Nicaragua.
We do not have armed conflicts in Canada, but I wish we had a more thorough discussion. Nevertheless, I am pleased to inform the Hon. Member that there is what I believe a good, modern precedent for the action the Government has taken at Meech Lake giving special consideration to one part of the population.

Madam Speaker, there was a notion advanced by some Hon. Members of the House that this would in fact increase federal power because spending power is in the Constitution. My reply to that is no, because it is in the common law and it would have been adopted by the courts if it had been litigated. I do not think we can argue that it is increasing federal power.

I was very interested in the remarks of the Hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco) who described dealing with a very similar problem at Trail in conjunction with Steel Workers' Local 480. I commend the Hon. Member for his part in the work that was done there. I commend the steel workers for their part in it as well.
I will describe a little of the difficulty that we had in approaching this problem. I was then the alderman for the ward concerned. The company concerned was Toronto Refiners and Smelters at the corner of Bathurst and Front

October 23, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
Streets. Within a year or so another company, Canada Metals, owned by the same outfit which owned the Trail smelter, Canada Pacific Investments, was causing the same problem two or three miles east at the foot of Pape Avenue.
We lacked almost entirely the legal tools needed to deal with that problem. We could not get action directly from the provincial Government, which at that time had jurisdiction over air quality. We had to use the local board of health. The local board of health, of course, has some very peremptory powers, but mostly on a different scale. It gives the medical officer of health power to order the repair or replacement of a faulty sanitary toilet if it is causing trouble to the neighbours. That does not go very far toward correcting a problem with a smelter.
When we directed the company, through the board of health, to stop spewing lead dust on to the neighbouring streets and houses in which people had been living before the plant was established, we were met with massive legal action. We were met with costs in the range of $100,000. Fortunately, the provincial Government allowed city council to reimburse three members of the board of health who were specifically acted against in a civil suit by a combination of the lead companies.
We learned that there is an international lead-zinc research organization which sends specialists throughout the world to testify, where necessary, that a little bit of lead does not really hurt you and to try to overshadow any local experts who may be able to show that there has been or is likely to be a harmful effect from the ingestion of lead, especially in children of preschool age.
We were finally able to make enough public fuss that the provincial Ministry of the Environment was pressured to take action in the matter. After several years it issued control orders requiring the companies to clean up to some extent. The problem has not been very well monitored and the pollution has continued, not at the same rate, but at a rate serious enough to require the replacement of the soil for the second time. Soil was replaced on the orders of the provincial Government because it was unfit to be on the property of families, especially those with small children. That was done at public expense rather than the expense of the company. The evidence now shows that the soil in some of those areas has been polluted a second time. Even though there was provincial legislation, the control has been very weak.
There was also a labour problem. Upon inquiry we found that in at least one plant workers who were tested by the company doctor for lead content in their blood were told not to worry, that they were okay. Not every family doctor has the knowledge or equipment to test for small quantities of lead in the blood. Therefore, we had some of them tested elsewhere, and the level of lead content found in their blood was medically shocking. They were shocked. They were quite unhappy at the thought that the company-paid doctor misled them. The fact is that the philosophy of the company doctor is that the patient is the company since it pays his bills. Therefore, he will
give the workers such information as the company wishes him to give them.
The workers in the plant found that not only was the neighbourhood being polluted, their health and lives were being endangered by lead. At that time we could find no help from the federal Government. However, I want to say, to the credit of the Speaker of the House, that in 1979 he was the Minister of the Environment and, in correspondence with me, indicated that he hoped to introduce a law that would enable the federal Government to take some action in cases like that. Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I move that Bill C-46 be read the third time and do pass. I want to take this opportunity to thank the members of the Legislative Committee on Bill C-46 for their good work.
I shall be brief. The purpose of Bill C-46 is to amend the Currency Act and the Royal Canadian Mint Act, so as to consolidate all technical matters pertaining to coins within one piece of legislation, to improve financial arrangements for the Mint and give it more operational flexibility, and finally, to simplify the marketing process for new projects approved in the Mint's corporate plan.
These changes are desirable to permit the Mint to continue its record of success, both commercially and technically.
As far as technical matters are concerned, it is desirable to allow the Mint to respond quickly to situations of metal shortages and to make minor changes in the size and composition of circulating coins. Any major changes in circulating coins will remain subject to the authority of Parliament.
All technical aspects of producing new coins will now be consolidated within the Royal Canadian Mint Act, while the Currency Act, under the authority of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), will be concerned only with matters relating to our monetary system.
Among the changes that will improve the financial and operational flexibility of the Mint is a provision that will permit the Mint to issue $40 million in shares which may be purchased by the Minister of Supply and Services.
These shares will provide the Mint with the funds it needs to meet its financing requirements. The Mint's borrowing authority will be raised from $35 million to $50 million, which may be borrowed from the private sector or the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
To provide further financial flexibility, the Mint will also be authorized to use its surplus operating capital to cover capital and other expenditures, instead of turning the surplus over to the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
The Bill also provides that the Government may authorize the Mint to produce precious metal coins to augment its series of gold coins.
The Mint will have the authority to borrow, rent or lease precious metals to ensure the interrupted production of coins such as the Maple Leaf.
Finally, the number of members sitting on the board of directors will be increased from seven to eleven, and it will no longer be necessary for three of those members to come from the Public Service. These changes will help provide all the expertise required for the proper functioning of an organization operating according to the rules of the market-place. Mr. Speaker, the principal mandate of the Royal Canadian Mint is to provide Canada with coins of the highest possible quality. However, the excellent record the Mint has acquired is also, if not primarely, due to its success in providing other products and services. These related activities have made the Royal Canadian Mint one of our most profitable Crown corporations on a year-to-year basis.
All the changes proposed in Bill C-46 will serve to give the Mint an up-to-date legislative environment that will permit it to continue its record of success.

Mr. Speaker, I will not take long. I know that this motion is to come to a vote, so I will end my remarks before six o'clock.
I did want to respond to some of the remarks made by Hon. members of the Opposition regarding the motion which is to declare Canada a nuclear weapons free zone. First, the motion calls for unilateral action. That really goes against the tradition of Canada and its security as a nation.

We cannot allow the concept of collective security to be destroyed by any
fragmentation in the idea of unilateralism for which this motion calls by declaring Canada a nuclear weapons free zone.
Second, the motion seems to assume that the most important issue in the world is peace. No one would deny that that is an incredibly important issue. All of us cherish the privilege of living in peace. In fact, I would underscore the fact that it is because we have had a collective security concept that we have been able to live in peace in this land.
The most important issue is not peace, it is freedom. There are many nations which are in peace. I can tell of the days I spent in East Germany. There is peace there, but it is not the kind of peace that I would enjoy. I have been in Bulgaria and there is peace there. I saw no war, no conflict, but it is not the kind of peace that I would enjoy. The most important privilege we have in this land is not peace but freedom. Hon. Members of the opposition Parties ought to appreciate that the most.
Third, the motion seems to assume that those with weapons are militarists. That is totally fallacious. The country that is the most militarily equipped and prepared in Europe today is not West Germany, France or Britain, it is Switzerland. Switzerland holds military manoeuvres every weekend and has its recruits in reserve, allowing them to take their weapons home from training. They keep their rifles in their homes. Who would say that Switzerland or Sweden for that matter, which is also militarily prepared, are militaristic because they believe in being militarily prepared?
We cannot accept this kind of motion. I recognize that it must come to a vote and it ought to. The House ought to express itself on this motion, but I hope it is roundly defeated, and I believe it will be because it deserves to be. We need to preserve not only the tradition of peace in this country but the tradition of freedom.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the speech made by my hon. colleague. I listened very intently and it occurred to me that it is more than appropriate that we take some time to consider the role of the Queen in respect to our nation and the Commonwealth to which this nation belongs.
A very interesting comparison can be made between this country and the United States. In contrast to Canada, they have in the United States in the same person the head of state and the head of Government. We know what great difficulties and confusion are caused by that state of affairs. That can be exemplified by the Watergate era. The then President of the United States, Richard Nixon, being both head of state and head of Government, caused a great deal of concern throughout the nation as to how to deal with the question of his actions as head of Government while at the same time he was symbolic of the American nation as a whole.
If we give a little thought to it, I am sure we would realize that there are a great many Canadians who would be very upset if our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) were at the same
time head of state and head of Government. It is convenient to have a clear separation.
Of course, in addition to being the head of our state represented by the Governor General, the Queen is also the symbolic head of the Commonwealth. The Commonwealth of Nations met in Vancouver not very long ago. At that time, I was pleased to have the occasion to meet the Queen under conditions in which we were able to exchange a few words as one person to another. I must say that I was quite impressed by her basic humanity and with the way she was able to converse with common people. In the final analysis, she has blood as red as ours flowing in her veins, and on that basis, with the exception of the symbol she constitutes, she is no different from the rest of us.
1 think it is important to talk about the Queen's position with respect to the Commonwealth. The Commonwealth is a group which shares the legacy of the British Empire and has eschewed the chains of imperialism to constitute a collectivity of nations which are bound together by their common heritage across racial, religious and ethnic lines. It is a voluntary grouping of nations.
If there is any other characteristic that ought to exist in the Commonwealth of Nations, it is that there should be an absence of any element of racism. Its mission should be to ensure that in this world, and certainly among the Commonwealth nations, there be no truck with racism.
Being aware of the Queen's position on the Commonwealth's treatment of the issue of apartheid, I was very pleased to learn that she is very concerned about the refusal of the British Government led by Margaret Thatcher to join with the rest of the Commonwealth in dealing with the issue of apartheid by making it possible for this noble collection of nations to exert its power and influence upon that dreadful regime to ensure that racism be eliminated there as it must be eliminated throughout the world. We are left in a rather curious situation. The Queen, the symbol of our nation and of the Commonwealth, resides in a country whose Prime Minister refuses to act in accordance with the traditions and concerns shared by so many of this great group of nations.
Rather than constructing a stone statue of the Queen, I think the greatest monument would be a Commonwealth which has been successful in establishing unity on this very serious problem which concerns so many. If the Commonwealth can act as Canada would lead it to act, then of course the greatest monument to the Queen would be a Commonwealth that is characterized by having taken for the first time effective actions to ensure that this legacy of racism colonialism has been left behind and will be eliminated once and for all. That is the kind of monument to build to the Queen.

Mr. Speaker, if you believe in public opinion polls you believe, as I do, that next to the economy and jobs the greatest concern of Canadians is with the environment. That is why the new Environmental Protection Act which the Government has introduced into Parliament, and which has received first and second reading and is finally before a legislative committee for consideration, is so important.
You know as well as I, Mr. Speaker, that that piece of legislation is only one of a good number of initiatives which the Government has undertaken in the last three years with regard to the environment. The initiatives taken include $40 million contributed by the federal Government and the provinces for the clean-up of the Windermere Basin in Hamilton Harbour as well as the Sydney tar ponds in Nova Scotia which is reputed to be the worst toxic chemical disposal site in eastern Canada.
In addition, the Government has entered into an agreement with the United States Government, Government of the State of New York, and the Government of the Province of Ontario to reduce the toxic chemicals which flow into the Niagara River by 50 per cent by 1996. The initiatives include as well a $2.3 million increase in the budget for pesticide controls and initiatives which have been taken on acid rain. The federal Government is contributing $335 million under agreements with the five eastern provinces to reduce acid rain emissions by one half by 1994.
In addition, new motor vehicle emission standards were introduced in September. An international agreement was reached at Montreal a short time ago on reducing damage to the ozone layer. As well, there will be $1.5 billion invested in the Canada-U.S. North American Waterfowl Management Plan. There is also the $1 million endangered species recovery fund.
Those are all initiatives which the Government has taken. In addition, five new national parks have been designated including the Pacific Rim Park at South Moresby in British Columbia, the Ellesmere Island Park in the Northwest Territories, the Bruce Peninsula Park in Ontario, and the Mingan Islands Park in Quebec. All of these initiatives have been undertaken in the last three years by the Government.
The Environmental Protection Act is another step. It, of course, deals with protecting the environment from new toxic pollution. That Bill is presently in committee and I am looking forward to seeing it passed so that it can help to protect Canadians from toxic chemicals in the future.
That is only one more step, Mr. Speaker. You, I, and the Parliamentary Secretary know that other things should be done as well to clean up the environmental problems which we have now.
November 3, 1987

What we really need on top of all these other things is a superfund like the one that was created in the United States, particularly for the purpose of cleaning up the problem areas in and around the Great Lakes.
There are some 45 industries in Canada that are polluting the Great Lakes. There are some 53 industries in the United States that are polluting the Great Lakes. There are some 10 hazardous waste sites in Canada that are leaking into the Great Lakes and 105 hazardous waste sites in the United States that are leaking into the Great Lakes. There are 32 municipalities in Canada that are polluting the Great Lakes and 81 municipalities in the United States that are polluting the Great Lakes.
We need a clean-up of all those industries, hazardous waste sites and the municipalities, especially the particularly hideous hazardous chemical dumps on the south side of the Niagara River in the United States. They include the Love Canal, High Park, 102nd Street and S Area dumps. All of them are causing enormous pollution.
There is much to be done. The Environmental Protection Bill which is now in committee is one more step in getting under way to solving the problems of the environment and cleaning up pollution. I hope tonight the Parliamentary Secretary will assure us that the Government will be pushing very hard to enact the Environmental Protection Bill into law and will then move on to these other major jobs of cleaning up the polluted areas that already exist in our environment.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak in support of this Bill which will replace the Livestock Pedigree Act with the Animal Pedigree Act, and which carries implications for the Canadian livestock industry which is such an important element in the economy of the constituency of Okanagan-Similkameen, the area I represent.
Since the Bill was tabled in June we have heard from industry representatives regarding modifications they would like made to the Bill before us. As a result of these interventions by industry leaders, the Minister has prepared draft amendments and has proposed that these draft amendments be considered later in committee.
We want to ensure that the best possible legislation is enacted to serve the pure-bred industry. Amendments to the Livestock Pedigree Act are long overdue. The old Act has been in force since 1900 and was last amended in 1952.
For almost 90 years the Livestock Pedigree Act has been regulating the activities of the 68 Canadian breed associations serving Canadian agriculture. The Animal Pedigree Act would update and replace the old Act with new legislation in order to better address today's realities in the livestock industry.
The main purpose of the Act is to promote breed improvement and to protect those raising or buying registered animals. It is estimated that the gains made in livestock productivity due to genetic improvement amount to roughly 1 per cent a year. That works out to be worth about $200 million a year for the Canadian livestock industry. Improved productivity has also enhanced our exports of Canadian breeding stock and semen. For example, in the past decade, Canadian exports of bovine semen have more than quadrupled. Recent figures show

November 5, 1987
Animal Pedigree Act
that exports of livestock and livestock products are worth well over $1 billion annually.
Livestock is an integral part of our agri-food system. There are solid economic reasons for the Government to ensure that the best possible livestock records are maintained. The new Animal Pedigree Act would retain the provisions of the old Act regarding animal pedigree associations authorized to keep pedigrees and to register animals of specific breeds. However, the new Act would also allow establishment of associations to keep records and to identify animals of evolving breeds. This is an important addition designed to encourage the best possible records and pedigrees of evolving breeds.
Livestock producers have been requesting these revisions for several years. The livestock industry has changed much since 1952. The new legislation is designed to meet today's requirements. The new Act will provide better protection to both buyers and sellers of livestock by strengthening Canada's livestock registration system.
1 would also like to point out that the provisions of the new Animal Pedigree Act, as contained in this Bill, have met with the full concurrence of the animal industry. Consultations with all sectors of the Canadian pure-bred animal breeding industry have been going on since 1982. Therefore, I am confident that this legislation will serve the animal industry well. In turn, it will be a real service to Canadian agriculture.
I will briefly outline the major new provisions contained in the Bill now before us. First, the new Animal Pedigree Act will more clearly define the basic purpose, powers and duties of animal pedigree associations. The new Act provides for the formation of the Canadian Livestock Records Corporation. This new corporation would replace the Canadian National Livestock Records which currently has the status of an affiliation whose legal powers and status are unclear. Third, the new Canadian Livestock Records Corporation would keep pedigrees for pure-bred animals and for animals in the process of evolving into new breeds. Any interested livestock association could avail itself of this service.
The Act also defines a pure-bred animal as having at least 87.5 per cent, that is seven-eighths, of its inheritance from one breed. However, additional associations could make this more restrictive if they so desired. The Act also provides for the recognition of new breeds of animals. It makes provisions for embryo transfers and artificial insemination.
The Act provides for the amalgamation and dissolution of breed associations. It also includes an expanded offences section. It specifies time limits for transferring certificates of registration or identification after a change of ownership, and sets penalties for exceeding those time limits. In addition, the level of fines under the new offences section is to be determined by the value of the animal to which the offence relates. The maximum level of fines under the new provision would be raised to $50,000 from the old $500 maximum set back in 1952.
The new Act also updates provisions under the old Act in line with current federal corporate law legislation. Taken together, these revisions will provide better protection for both buyer and seller of registered or identified animals. In fact, the revisions will strengthen Canada's livestock registration system and could potentially increase world demand for Canadian livestock.
In summary, the Animal Pedigree Act will provide greater protection for the buyer of livestock, more realistic penalties for violations of the Act and more flexible rules for breed organization. This is a long awaited piece of legislation which deserves the support of this House.

We have raised our concerns a number of times, both in the House and in the committee, about the extent as well as the area to be covered in the public hearings to be held by the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade.

Madam Speaker, under the Public Order Emergency Part, which is Part II of Bill C-77, there are some very strong measures introduced to be put into practice. It is important that we are not conned into thinking that Part II, Public Order Emergency, is a light piece of legislation. It is very strong in its statements. It certainly infringes on civil liberties to a great extent. If we go on to the International Emergency Part, we find that the declaration outlines the state of affairs. It is very strong. Part III, Clause 25, reads:
"international emergency" means an emergency involving Canada and one or more other countries that arises from acts of intimidation or coercion or the real or imminent use of serious force or violence and that directly threatens the sovereignty, security or territorial integrity of Canada or any of its allies or any other country in which the political, economic or security interests of Canada or any of its allies are involved.
While we have an alliance to which we belong, the legislative committee will have to look very carefully at this clause under "International Emergency" which can drag Canada into a conflict as a result of another country's activities or problems.
You will know that when the War Measures Act was invoked in 1970, Madam Speaker, it expressly overrode the Bill of Rights. Furthermore, we had no Charter at that time. We now have a Charter. Let me point out that if the Diefen-baker Government in 1960 had not specifically stated that the Bill of Rights did not override the War Measures Act we would have had those measures controlling the War Measures Act in 1970. It is, therefore, understandable that my Leader lamented having to use the Act, precisely because there was no check on the exercise of its powers. That situation no longer exists today and it will not exist under this legislation.
I want to quote a statement which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) made in the House on October 16, 1970. During the debate on the war measures legislation at that time he said:
The rule of law is the essential condition not only for the existence of the state but for the existence of individual liberty within the state. Freedom is the precondition of liberty, and restraint is the beginning of freedom. The rule of law is the source and condition of that restraint, and through it the freedom and the liberty of the individual in society are maintained.
Insurrection and violence are not only a total denial of the constituted authority of the state but are a denial of the liberty of the individual himself who depends upon the controlled organization of the state. This type of violence defies not only the total integrity of society as a people but the individual integrity of every person in that society.
An important part of this legislation is that Part 11, Public Order Emergency, if strictly enforced, gives a cruel Government, a huge Government or a Government emotionally motivated rather than rationally motivated, maybe trying to get political points by a show of force, the basis for that Government to act. This particular section of the Bill is one that we will have to look at very carefully while scrutinizing the legislation in a legislative committee.
I want to say to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty)-and this is no reflection on him as a person in any way whatever, but from comments I have been getting, the populace would feel a little more relieved if the administration of Bill C-77 when it becomes legislation were under a Minister of the Government other than the Minister of National Defence. As I say, there is nothing personal read into that, but just an uneasiness that some people feel.
The fairness that must be built into this legislation is extremely important. While the War Measures Act was important to the free world during the crises of World War I and World War II, let us keep in mind those people we recently remembered at the cenotaphs across the country who fought and died by the tens of thousands to leave behind a Canada on which the rest of us could build. It is extremely important today that we remember them and the Canada which they wanted for the future.
We must consider what must be done in this Bill to accommodate the civil liberties, the property rights and the freedom of Canadians, whether it be during wartime or peacetime, so that under the part dealing with compensation those people be given the right to get compensation on an equal basis before the courts of Canada.
One writer discussing this Bill has stated:
Those whose liberties-or property-were harmed would be given the right to compensation.
The only worry here is that a section of the Bill provides a long list of regulations under which the Cabinet could define the ambit of compensation. A mean-spirited Government, or one intent on post facto justifications for its actions, could make compensation unnecessarily limited by restrictive regulations. On November 3, 1987 the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais) raised a question of privilege with regard to the conduct of the Hon. Member for LaSalle (Mr. Lanthier) at the meeting of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, which was held on October 7, 1987 for the purpose of electing a Chairman of the committee pursuant to Standing Orders 91 and 92.

I had indicated that I might come back to the House to hear further comments, but when looking at Hansard for that day, I found everything I needed to make a ruling on the matter today. I wish to thank the Hon. Members who took part in this procedural debate for their interventions.
November 18, 1987



The Hon. Member for La Prairie maintains that the Hon. Member for LaSalle misled the committee by stating that he had relinquished the position of Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works on the day of his election, namely, October 7, 1987, when he offered his candidacy as Chairman of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. He furthered claimed that the Hon. Member for LaSalle was being paid an additional amount of salary awarded to Parliamentary Secretaries as shown in the Public Accounts of 1986-1987 on page 12.9 for the period covering October 15, 1986 to October 16, 1987. The Hon. Member for La Prairie seems to imply that this somehow made the Hon. Member for LaSalle ineligible for that chairmanship.

The Hon. Member for LaSalle replied that he had told the Minister of Public Works and other people about his resignation from the position of Parliamentary Secretary at a meeting on October 6, 1987, and that, that same day, he had written a letter of resignation to the Prime Minister indicating his intention to seek the chairmanship of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. He also pointed out that, as he was Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works and not to the Minister of Labour or the Minister of Employment and Immigration, even if he had kept his position of Parliamentary Secretary, there would clearly have been no conflict in his seeking the chairmanship of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. However, he formally stated that he had resigned and gave as evidence of this fact his letter to the Prime Minister.

The receipt of the additional amounts of money as Parliamentary Secretary did not cause concern to the Hon. Member for LaSalle because, he argued, adjustments will be made as soon as the change in his status affecting his salary is made known to the appropriate authorities.
I wish to underline to all Hon. Members the role of the Speaker with respect to a question of privilege raised by any Member of the House. The Speaker simply determines whether a prima facie case of breach of privilege has occurred. If he so finds, the motion moved by the Hon. Member raising the matter is immediately proposed to the House by the Chair and thus all other business is set aside until that motion is disposed of by the House. It is for the House to decide the matter and not the Speaker.

After examining the reports carefully, for several reasons, I cannot find a prima facie case of privilege.

As to the issue of the Hon. Member for LaSalle being a Parliamentary Secretary and whether or not he was eligible to be the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Labour,
Privilege-Mr. Jourdenais
Employment and Immigration, Standing Order 89(2) has a note which was adopted by the House in June of this year. That note reads:

For the purpose of this Standing Order, a Parliamentary Secretary shall not be a member of a standing committee which has in its mandate the review of a department to which the said Parliamentary Secretary is attached.
This note should be sufficient to settle the matter as the Hon. Member for LaSalle was Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works and not to the Minister of Labour or the Minister of Employment and Immigration. There was therefore no objection to his being elected chairman of the Committee.

Further, the Hon. Member for LaSalle has told the House that he had in any case resigned his parliamentary secretaryship. We have so much tradition in this area that I do not need or intend to cite the authorities about accepting the word of an Hon. Member.

I note on page 10687 of Hansard for November 3, 1987, that the Hon. Member for La Prairie moved the following motion:
That the question of the behaviour of the Hon. Member for LaSalle (Mr. Lanthier) be referred to the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure, and in the meantime I would ask you to invite the Hon. Member for LaSalle to relinquish the chairmanship.
May I point out that it is not sufficient to make a charge in general terms with regard to the conduct of another Member. Such charges should contain specific accusations. I would like to remind all Members of the long established traditions of the House, and its committees, that an inquiry with respect to the conduct of a Member can only take place provided that he has been charged with a specific offence or offences.

I think that it is especially important to remind all Hon. Members of the comments made by Speaker Michener in his often-quoted ruling on the Pallett case on June 19, 1949. These comments can be found on page 584 of the Journals'.

In my view simple justice requires that no Hon. Member should have to submit to investigation of his conduct by the House or a committee until he has been charged with an offence.
Such a procedure or requirement is the only means of ensuring fairness, and Speaker Michener was clear that Members are as entitled to such protection as is every ordinary Canadian citizen.
Therefore, I must rule that there is no prima facie case of privilege in this matter.

I have another ruling with respect to a matter raised on October 13 by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), who raised a question of privilege alleging improper restrictions on the rights of the members of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. Supported by several other Members, the Hon. Member objected specifically to the adoption by the committee of the following motion:
That during the course of the evaluation of the Committee's researchers and research needs, no Member of the Committee engage any of the researchers without the consent of the Chairman.

Just before the motion at issue, it had been agred to proceed to an evaluation of the committee's research needs.

On October 13,1 told the House that I did not think that the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt had a question of privilege. I said that perhaps he had a complaint. After studying the precedents and the authorities I can now confirm that my first view of the matter was indeed correct. There is no prima facie question of privilege to be found in the issue raised by the Hon. Member.

Previous rulings and parliamentary custom are quite clear. Committees are definitely in control of their own procedures. In this respect, I may refer Hon. Members to Beauchesne's, Fifth Edition, Citation 569(3), which reads as follows:

The Speaker has ruled on many occasions that it is not competent for him to exercise procedural control over the committees. Committees are and must remain masters of their own procedure.
On May 3, 1972, Mr. Speaker Lamoureux had the following to say about a problem in a committee that was raised in the House:
I think it is long-established practice that difficulties in discussions and debates in a committee should be settled by the committee itself, and that if there are difficulties which are to be considered by the House this should be done at the time the report of the committee is before the House for debate and consideration by the members of the House.
In addition to these points there is in my mind a question of the propriety and practicality of having the proceedings of one committee investigated by another committee of the House. I can foresee all sorts of difficulties if this were allowed and became a practice of the House.
That is a quote from the judgment of Mr. Speaker Lamoureux on May 3, 1972.

According to established custom, the proceedings of committees may not be considered or debated in the House except in the form of a committee report. If a point of order or question of privilege is raised in a committee, the matter should be dealt with in committee rather than being raised in the House.
Traditionally, the conduct of a Member may not be submitted for scrutiny to the House by way of a question of privilege.

The Speaker went on in the same ruling to say that he had:
-always had serious doubts of the advisability of having proceedings of a committee investigated by another committee of the House.
I would also cite Mr. Speaker Jerome on May 26, 1975, when he stated:
First, both Members at one time or another suggested that the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections ought to have these questions referred to it, which to me would seem to establish a precedent and initiate or encourage a practice wherein the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections would become some kind of court of appeal on the proceedings of other standing committees. It seems to me that nothing could be more unacceptable as a practice which ought to be more directly discouraged.
I can refer Hon. Members to many rulings that are similar and make the same point.
I thus feel that our precedents are clear and repeat, with regret, that I cannot find that the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt has made out a prima facie question of privilege.
I should also add that, perhaps appropriately, the Chair has been lenient in hearing complaints that may have come forward as a question of privilege or point of order from committees. I have done so because the committees have new powers and are finding their way. Perhaps by hearing some of those matters, it has assisted all Hon. Members to make the committee system work more satisfactorily.
I would ask Hon. Members to keep in mind that the leniency of the Chair for a while ought not to be pressed too far, and especially because of that I have taken a few minutes to put some of the procedural law, which is our tradition, before the House. I would ask Hon. Members to strive mightily to resolve their problems in committee before they feel it necessary to come to the Chair on those matters.

As we know, this Bill is quite simple. Its purpose is to ensure that the official designation of Nova Scotia remains "Nova Scotia" in legal acts in both French and English. The reason given by the sponsor is quite logical. When King James I gave that land to Sir William Alexander in 1621, the act of transfer designated the land under the Latin name of "Nova Scotia". The Hon. Member pointed out that, while official bilingualism leads us to translate certain geographic names from French to English and vice versa, we have no reason to do so for Latin names, no more than for the many native words which are so characteristic of the geographic designations in this country.
In terms of linguistics, since this is really what concerns us here, I would first like to mention that when the term "Nou-velle-Ecosse" is used in French, it is not meant to be a Translation of the term "Nova Scotia". Rather, I would say that it is the manner in which the French language refers to the same reality, just as it does in the case of many other realities, geographic or other. For example, when one uses the term "Germany", also of Latin origin, in English, or the term "Allemagne", which is also derived from Latin, in French with the same meaning, one does not usually stop to think that the Germans themselves call their country Deutschland. Obviously, the same can be said of a great number of other countries and regions of the world. What would be at the root of such a strange phenomenon? I cannot really say and in fact I would rather leave that to linguists and etymologists. However, I believe that even a layman can draw a few useful conclusions in terms of this debate.
The example I have just given shows that if geographic names can be so different from one language to the next it would seem to be mainly for historical reasons, given the fact that the terms "Allemagne", "Germany" and "Deutschland" have absolutely nothing in common except that they refer to the same reality. It seems also that the strength of usage and tradition as well as a certain emotional dimension, which may of course vary from one culture to another, also play a major role. I would even go further and add that the various designations which have stood the test of time are often the mark of the historical fame which those territories have gained. It could be said that cultures acknoweledge one another in this way. Even if we are dealing here with proper nouns, these terms have become part and parcel of a language.

Mr. Speaker, the 1981 Census statistics showed that almost 50 per cent more immigrant women than men had no knowledge of either official language. The main reason for this deplorable statistic is the federal Government's policy on subsidized language training for immigrants. This policy clearly disadvantages women. Immigrant women, who may not be working in the labour force, are certainly working in the home and they need to communicate in one of the official languages to function efficiently in their daily lives.
Immigrant women who are seeking to enter the workforce are also often denied access to language training, as it is judged that the few marketable job skills they possess will make them ineligible for employment that requires communication abilities.
The result is that immigrant women, especially those from developing countries, are ghettoized in low-paying menial jobs. We know that this only reinforces the sexist and the racist stratification of our society that keeps women of visible minority groups in poverty, and powerless in our society.

This Bill would abolish therapeutic abortion committees and allow qualified medical practitioners to perform abortions without having to get the prior authorization of these committees. Do we have the power to say, then, that this is not a life? The same holds true for the unborn child.

is not an extension of the mother anymore than the astronaut is an extension of the spaceship.
The Member who introduced this Bill is from my home province and should be aware of the abortion statistics for B.C. We do not have a record we can be proud of. In fact, the figures are frightening. B.C.'s abortion rate just two years ago, in 1985, was over 50 per cent higher than the national average. That means that for every 100 live births in B.C., 26.1 abortions are performed. Mr. Speaker, we are presently debating Bill C-87, an Act respecting a harmonized tariff system and, in particular, Motions Nos. 4 and 12. Our concern with this Act is much greater under the circumstances surrounding the Mulroney-Reagan trade agreement than it would ordinarily have been. the harmonized coding system for trade. However, the Bill becomes much more important under the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal because it will have a much greater impact than it would under ordinary circumstances. It therefore requires much closer scrutiny than would ordinarily have been given it.
As a result of the trade agreement certain tariffs will be put into effect almost immediately upon the signing of the agreement. Things which were routine in the past must now be questioned as a result of that agreement. Motions Nos. 4 and 12 are aimed at greater accountability of the Cabinet to Parliament. At present the Government can impose a tariff and ask for ratification of it by Parliament 180 days later. The barons faced King John because they wanted to go before the King more than once every two or three years to hear how much money he needed and what he needed it for.
The Government can now impose a tax on the people of Canada and need only ask Parliament for permission to do so more than a year later. The recommended changes in Clauses 32 and 61 would increase the responsibility of Cabinet to Parliament. Rather than being able to impose taxes and collect them for a year before having them ratified by Parliament, these amendments suggest that we reduce that time period to 60 days.
The Mulroney-Reagan trade agreement has brought the need for the accountability of the Cabinet to Parliament to the forefront. At present such an agreement can be signed by the Prime Minister, and the Government can bring forward a Ways and Means motion to impose or remove tariffs. That decision to impose or remove such tariffs will remain in effect for an entire year and, quite often, more than a year.
Our present year is 177 days. This Bill, at present, allows 180 days to be used up before the Government must come back to Parliament and have it ratified. Therefore, more than a year, at least 15 days into the next year, will be required before it is necessary to pass it. It seems wrong, in the view of democrats all over the world, to have a treaty signed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the President of the United States, to be put in place and negotiated by people who are not Members of Parliament, nor representatives of the people, a treaty which will abrogate the laws not only of the Parliament of Canada, because those tariffs were put in place by the Parliament of Canada, but also the laws of the legislatures of the provinces.
This treaty about which we are talking, or any kind of treaty or any Ways and Means motion which changes taxes, customs and excise taxes, does so without compunction and can do so, leaving those changes in place for a whole year before they have to come to Parliament for ratification. A treaty does not have to be accountable to Parliament. It can take off a tariff

which was put in place by Parliament, and it can be established technically as the law of the land just by the Government presenting the House with a motion which says that this is the action it intends to take.
Sometimes this motion is not even in the form of a Ways and Means motion, but in the form of a little line in a statement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) as to what he is going to do in the next year in his Budget. The 180 days really means that the will of Parliament has been sidelined. If we establish that tariff in Parliament, it is the will of Parliament that it be there. On Wednesday November 25, 1987, the Hon. Member for Broadview Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) raised in the House the manner in which her Private Member's Bill C-204 is being dealt with in the legislative committee appointed to study the Bill.

The Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) claimed that the Committee's proceedings were being systematically obstructed by Government Members sitting on the Committee and by the Committee's Chairman or Acting Chairman. She said that Government Members did not look favourably on the Bill and that the actions of the Acting Chairman on Thursday, November 24, 1987, reflected his prejudice against the Bill before the Committee.

I wish to thank the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazan-kowski) and the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. St. Germain) for their contribution to this important matter. The Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. James) must

I wish to remind all Hon. Members of my ruling of November 18, 1987, where I cited several excerpts from the rulings of my predecessors concerning the established custom and traditions of the House in not interfering in committee proceedings until such committees have reported to the House. This is an important rule that has clear underpinnings in logic, and I, of course, want to follow it.
Thus, after careful consideration, I have come to the conclusion that the Hon. Member's complaint ought properly to be dealt with in committee and, therefore, it is not a question of privilege and cannot be dealt with here unless the matter is reported to the House by the committee.
There are established practices which have been followed for a long time. One is that Members refrain from criticizing the actions of another Member without the making of a clear charge set out in a motion. The traditional and proper way of dealing with the type of conduct alleged by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood would be by appealing the conduct of the chairman to the committee, or by way of a motion proposed to the committee and, if it is adopted, reporting the same to the House.

I hope that in future, Hon. Members will be guided by what I said on November 18, 1987 and will formulate their complaints and grievances in the committees, which are entirely capable of dealing with these matters, instead of wasting the precious time of the House. The precedents are clear: These questions do not come under the jurisdiction of the Chair.

Two or three of them went together and pooled their quotas in order to get a car, because the elevators were plugged. Out of 150 some permit book holders at the shipping point at which I was located, there were over 100 cars on order by one or more individual producers, so that they could load railway cars on their own. It had to be done over the loading platform with their grain augers. Some of them even used shovels.
Well, Mr. Speaker, what happened? Most of those 100 cars at our little shipping point were met over the course of the crop
December 9, 1987

year, or the remainder of the crop year. But the railroad said, "This shipping point has had so many cars, as many or more than other shipping points have had". The next thing we knew, a week or two before the end of the crop year, the elevators were plugged and the quota had been raised from five bushels to seven bushels per acre. One of the elevator agents of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, the last two days of the crop year, July 30, went out and bought about 50 rolls of tar-paper. He spread it out on the ground down by the stockyards. He phoned all his wheat pool members and said, "Bring in your last two bushels per acre". We ended up with 57,000 bushels piled on the ground on top of the tar-paper. Then the railroads had to provide an additional 25 cars to pick that grain up off the ground.

This additional tax grab has negative effects on many sectors of the economy. Furthermore, this measure cannot be judged in isolation. One must also examine the other increases in indirect taxes introduced by the Conservative Government.
Let us consider the Conservative record when it comes to increases in indirect taxes, that is to say, sales and excise taxes. First, let us look at gasoline and associated products. visible minorities in the Public Service, targets that had never been in place before.

I might not have been particularly concerned if it had come from only one or two sources, but I have had those concerns raised to me by people who work in the Department of Justice, people who work in the Department of Supply and Services, people who work in the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, people who work in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, people who work in Treasury Board itself, people who work in the Department of Employment and Immigration, people who work in the Department of Labour, people who work in the Department of the Environment, and people who work for the Public Service Commission of Canada, which is supposed to be there to make sure that everybody receives equal treatment.
These people tell me that the programs which have been put in place are not working. In fact, they say that instead of actually increasing the number of visible minorities in the Public Service, they are actually decreasing because of retirements and lay-offs. After years of the former Liberal Government doing nothing about seeing that visible minorities in the Public Service were promoted to management and senior management positions, they had hoped that with this Government there would be a change. Member that one of the jobs of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is to ensure that federal Government decision-makers know that these enterprises exist and what they do and that national policies and programs reflect an awareness of these facts.
I would suggest that previous administrations have been deficient in doing so. The agency will also keep on top of what other federal Departments and agencies do and plan to do in order to ensure that those plans, if they have a bearing on Atlantic Canada, meet the aims of the agency. It will not take too long for other Departments to become aware that there is an advocate for Atlantic Canada, contrary to the remarks of the Hon. Member. That advocate is the federal Government, this federal Government. It will not be long before federal activity in Atlantic Canada is more unified and joint action by Departments and agencies commonplace.

January 18, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
A unique feature of this Bill reinforces the Minister's coordination activities. That is Clause 9. That part of the Bill states that when the Minister is satisfied that the implementation of a program or project authorized by any other Act would further the purpose of the agency, the Minister may conditionally or unconditionally undertake to transfer funds appropriated for the purpose of ACOA to supplement funds that the Minister responsible for the program or project has undertaken to expend. This unique co-financing provision means that the Minister for ACOA can transfer ACOA funds to another federal project or program if that will help ACOA meet its objectives.
That means that ACOA will not have to develop its own programs where there may be programs administered by another Department that will be doing the same job. It means that if there is a progam that would help ACOA foster economic growth in the region, but the program cannot be extended or fully used in Atlantic Canada because of a funding problem, ACOA can then add funds so the program can benefit Atlantic Canada.
The co-ordination and co-financing inherent in the Bill gives the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency the flexibility it must have to pursue its purpose of economic growth in the region.

Member square that with the fact that he was a member of the Cabinet of the Government during the period of time when infrastructure was being touted as the way for restructuring, refinancing, and making Atlantic Canada independent of the regional disparity that we see there today? Speech:
Mr. Speaker, on December 14 I raised a question with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) with respect to the settlement of the Air Canada strike. That strike being settled notwithstanding, I wish to return to the subject because of the wide implications that strikes and lock-outs have for the consumers of Canada as well as for labour and management.
Very frequently we think the only parties to a labour dispute are the employers and the employees, but the people very often most affected by a work stoppage are members of the consuming public. Think of the strikes we have had in the past 12 months in Canada which have had a direct bearing upon customers, members of the public. There was the police strike in Saint John, New Brunswick, the teachers' strike in Metropolitan Toronto, the Canada Post strike across the nation, the strike in Prince Rupert which closed the grain terminal and has brought a great loss to the farmers of western Canada.
I quote from a newspaper report concerning the impact of the Canada Post strike on small businesses. The writer said "Small firms, always the most vulnerable during economic disruptions, are starting to feel the pinch from the three week old postal dispute".
Over and over again we are aware that a strike or lock-out not only hits hard the people on the picket line or in the offices of the companies involved, it hits hard the people who are depending upon the flow of supplies and services, the people who are the members of the consuming public and have some right to be served, a right that is often denied them by the two participants in the dispute.
Tonight I raise the questions: who looks after the consuming public? Who cares about the customer? Who cares about the member of the public who has apparently no rights at all in a labour dispute except the right to wait passively and independently for two other parties to settle a dispute that so profoundly affects his or her life? It seems to me that it is time for Governments to take this very seriously. If they do not speak up and act on behalf of the consuming public, who will?
January 18, 1988

I would urge the Governments of Canada to consider very seriously a conference involving both the Canadian Government and the provinces together with representatives of management and labour so that there could be some consensus built for an alternative to the strike as the ultimate weapon. 1 say that the strike is now out of date. There are much better alternatives. Some of them have been tried in other countries. There are labour courts and various forms of arbitration. All these deserve some further and more serious consideration within Canada so that justice can be done for people who have so long been denied it and who have a right to be heard. I plead with the Parliament of this land to hear their plea and to act for them. If we do not, who will?

Let us consider the example of other countries. Sweden has had social democratic government for 45 of the last 50 years. The profits of these companies over two generations have been astronomical. Yet what have they done for this country? As a result of their negligence and refusal to co-operate in planting trees to replace those that they cut down, they have brought the industry to the point where, according to industry sources themselves, we will be facing a major catastrophe in the next couple of generations.

Research on substitutes to ensure and secure an orderly transition to chemicals and products which will not adversely affect our ozone layer remains a critical element in the timely resolution of this problem. I am happy to be able to report that an unprecedented level of research is now moving forward on several fronts.

Alternatives are being sought in three areas: alternative chemicals; products and services; and technologies.

Madam Speaker, at the time of Confederation the country was preoccupied with the mechanics of unification and asserting a unique identity among the family members of world nations.
After Confederation Canada grew steadily, but in an orderly fashion. It was not until 1917, 50 years after Confederation, that we finally established our true independence in the eyes of the rest of the world. During that year, at the Battle of Vimy Ridge, Canadians served for the first time as a wholly Canadian force, emerging with distinction as victors. Other nations at that point came to regard us as an autonomous nation with our own strengths, Government and national character.
At that time the red ensign graced flagpoles around our nation, side by side with the Union Jack. As the years passed the Parliament and people of Canada expressed the desire that we have a new flag that would be readily identified as a symbol of Canada throughout the world. Some people today are sorry that there is not a bit of blue in that flag because it is my understanding that blue stands for integrity, white stands for peace, and red stands for sacrifice.
Adjournment Debate
Our own red and white banner of freedom and equality, with the distinctive Canadian maple leaf, was adopted by Parliament in 1964 and officially proclaimed on February 15, 1965, by the Queen. There are Members here today who were serving in Parliament at that time and I am certain each one of them remembers that day with fondness and pride.
Again, a fair amount of time passed before we obtained our own Constitution in 1982, but with the careful planning that went into that completely Canadian document we ended up with the finest and fairest declaration of self-identity in the world. We do things gradually, but we do get them right.
Madam Speaker, the story of our national anthem as well parallels such timely growth. Its inception dates back to 1880 when the French Canadian composer Calixa Lavallee wrote the music to a French text by Mr. Justice Routhier at the request of the Lieutenant Governor of Quebec. For a while English Canadians would still sing God Save the Queen or The Maple Leaf Forever.
In 1908 the Hon. Robert Stanley Weir penned the English version which, over the years, was given recognition by federal and provincial Governments for ceremonial occasions. Forty years later this became the official anthem of the Canadian Armed Forces by way of Order in Council.
Finally, in 1980, the 100th anniversary year of the music, our House of Commons adopted a Bill proclaiming O Canada as our legal, official national anthem. We have fondness for centennials in Canada, Madam Speaker.
These inspiring lines still make our hearts swell with pride when we see our flag wave, when our athletes excel in international competition, and when we travel to foreign lands and hear people speak with such respect for this nation we call home.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question of the Hon. Member who has had a substantial interest in this issue. Hon. Members will recall that one of the important conclusions of the Deschenes Commission, in light of the fact that it was not in a position to travel and hold hearings overseas or behind the Iron Curtain, was that there should be established safeguards with respect to the taking of evidence and the terms of investigations of alleged crimes. We as a Government, and I on behalf of the Government, accepted the recommendations of the Deschenes Commission.

We did not hear from the Minister of Finance in his statement-that is all it was, a dry run for an election-about what role Canada was playing in
the world. We did not hear about what position we were going to take on Third World debt or the position we were going to take at the IMF or the World Bank about refinancing that debt. February 25, 1988
Adjournment Debate

Speech:
I am sure that the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. Benjamin) will take part in this debate, and 1 know that he will support the legislation designed to bring benefit to his constituents as well as mine.
There have been several organizational experiments over the past 60 years to promote regional and economic development in Canada. I would suggest that there has been little measurable progress.
One thing that has been clear from those experiments is that Ottawa-based centralized approaches fail to capture the regional differences that we all recognize in Canada. They failed to provide federal policies which are tailored to the individual needs of the men and women in each region of Canada. The West's development problems are not the same as those of Atlantic Canada, northern Ontario, or Quebec.
When this Government came to office we came with ideas of how to make regional development work. We made a commitment to ensure that the regions of Canada would have a strong voice in influencing economic development.
The first half of this mandate was designed to create the right environment, the economic growth, and the investment that was needed. It was also designed to correct some sectorial inadequacies that were apparent, such as those in energy, agriculture, taxation, trade, and in other sectors. The groundwork has been done and the base has been established. Regional development can only take place when the climate for national economic development is right.
Once the climate was created, new tools for regional economic development were put in place. In June the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced the creation of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency; in July the Northern Ontario Development Fund was announced; and on August 4, 1987 the Prime Minister announced the new western diversification initiative. These are regional initiatives, and they are major undertakings to correct regional imbalances and inadequacies.
In the past under DREE, DRIE, and all the others, of which there have been several, regional economic development policy and regional economic program delivery were never successfully married.
The legislation before the House at this time brings the policy development and the program delivery together. The policy role, which would be combined with the instruments of the Western Economic Development Fund, will allow us to have the tools to do the job.
A major component of the initiative is the department with headquarters in Edmonton and offices in Winnipeg, Saskatoon, and Vancouver. It is to promote diversification from regional ideas. It is not an Ottawa-imposed approach to the economic development of the West. It is close to the people whom it is designed to serve. It is not located in Ottawa, but in the West. It will also bring a western voice to the formation of national policy. All Ministers, regardless of their ministry responsibilities, always speak on behalf of their regions and will continue to do that. What we are doing now is putting in statute and legislating a department which will speak and attempt to influence national policies in order that those national policies can better serve people in western Canada.
When we look at the areas that are important, to mention some, agriculture, forestry, transport, science and technology, it is important to draw those agencies and departments together and to examine the programs and the policies in relation to the economic development potential in western Canada.
I believe there is an opportunity to influence Government without expenditures. As an example, in the August Budget we were able to work as a pathfinder where kaolin was classified as a mineral. That is the first change in the schedule since potash was recognized as a mineral some 20 years ago. It seems strange to me, since it was not a vegetable and it was mined out of the ground, that it was not classified as a mineral. It had to be classified as a mineral in order that the tax regime available to mining could be put in place. That was recognized by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and announced in the Budget of February 10.
I do not think it is misstating a fact, and my colleague from Saskatchewan will recognize it, but it is almost twice as far from Ottawa to Regina than it is from Regina to Ottawa. That is a fact of life that we have recognized for a long period of time.
The department will work as a pathfinder for those men and women in western Canada who have ideas and proposals, who want to do business with the Government of Canada, and who want to assist us in strengthening the economy in the West. It will serve as a voice in western Canada to promote cooperative ventures with the provinces, business, labour, and other public and private organizations. The department will also have the following responsibilities. It will formulate plans and integrate federal strategies to support the economic diversification of the western economy. It will oversee or implement such plans and strategies, if they are not implemented by other Ministries. It will promote the growth of small and medium-sized businesses. It will attempt to improve the business environment in western Canada. It will support economic and policy research. Finally, it will engage in and conclude co-operative arrangements with the provinces.
March 1, 1988
